statement: As described in a narrative review (Angarita et al., 2016; figures second-hand, no systematic search or appraisal), cannabis can make it easier to fall asleep with short-term use, but people who use it regularly become tolerant to this, and stopping regular use is followed by sleep problems: cited studies found sleep difficulties in 32 to 76% of people in cannabis withdrawal, strange or vivid dreams starting within days of stopping and sometimes lasting weeks, and in sleep-laboratory studies longer time to fall asleep, more waking, less total and deep sleep, and a rebound of REM sleep, more marked in people who had used heavily. Poor sleep during abstinence was linked with relapse; sleep improved again with THC or a return to cannabis, but the review notes that regular use itself worsens sleep over time, and going back to cannabis, alcohol or other sedatives to get to sleep was commonly observed. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: A review of sleep research says that cannabis can help some people fall asleep at first, but people who use it every day get used to that effect. When they stop, many sleep badly and have strange dreams for days or weeks. Poor sleep was linked with going back to cannabis. These are second-hand findings from a review that did not check study quality.
population: People who use cannabis regularly and stop, in studies cited by a narrative review
exposure: Stopping regular cannabis use (withdrawal and abstinence)
comparator: Their own sleep at baseline or during use, or healthy sleepers, as in the cited studies
outcome: Self-reported sleep problems and dreams, polysomnographic sleep, relapse
magnitude: Second-hand, as summarized: sleep difficulties in 32 to 76% of people experiencing withdrawal, in studies of up to 450 participants; strange dreams starting within days and lasting up to about six weeks in some studies; polysomnography in withdrawal with longer sleep onset, more waking, reduced total sleep, efficiency and slow-wave sleep, and REM rebound.

evidence.extracted: As summarized: cannabis may improve subjective sleep in short-term use; with chronic use, withdrawal brings sleep difficulty, strange dreams, insomnia and poor sleep quality, in 32% to 76% of people experiencing withdrawal, in inpatient and outpatient studies and placebo-controlled discontinuation studies; strange dreams typically begin within days of stopping and can persist for weeks; returning to cannabis, alcohol or other sedatives to sleep is commonly observed; the sleep-promoting effect is lessened in chronic users compared with naive users.

evidence.locator: Cannabis › Objective measurements, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Table 2
evidence.extracted: As summarized: tolerance develops to the sleep-inducing and slow-wave effects with chronic use; polysomnography in withdrawal shows increased sleep onset latency and waking, reduced total sleep time, efficiency and slow-wave sleep, and REM rebound; changes can start as soon as the first night, are more noticeable in heavy use, progress over the first weeks and persist into abstinence.

evidence.locator: Cannabis › Clinical and laboratory correlates of subjective and objective sleep outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Pharmacotherapy options targeting sleep abnormalities, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: As summarized: higher relapse rates were correlated with sleep problems and other withdrawal symptoms, and poor sleep during abstinence contributes to relapse; withdrawal sleep disturbances improve with oral THC or resumption of cannabis use, but the beneficial effects of THC on sleep diminish with chronic use and chronic use leads to more severe sleep problems.
Narrative, non-systematic review; no selection criteria, numbers or appraisal.

risk_of_bias.note: Cited studies not appraisable through a narrative review.

inconsistency.note: REM findings in longer abstinence conflict; the main directions are consistent as described.

indirectness.note: Second-hand figures from a narrative review.

grade.reasoning: Observational and laboratory discontinuation studies seen only through a narrative review: start low, rated down for risk of bias and indirectness (METHODS 6.3). Stays draft. Status replicated as described: many cited studies, inpatient and outpatient, in the same direction.
